I Bought My Mom 6 Pairs of Shoes. She Wore One.

Before you buy her another pair she will thank you for and never wear.

Ellen Brandt

Ellen spent nineteen years running the front desk of a physiotherapy clinic, which is where she learned that the shoe people arrive in tells you more than the form they fill out.

Her mother lives an hour up the highway, on her own, and means to keep it that way. Ellen writes about the small purchases that make that possible, and the ones that end up in a box.

In four years I bought my mother memory-foam sneakers, two pairs from the orthopedic place her doctor named, a wide-fit pair out of a catalog, and walking shoes she picked herself and wore exactly twice.

Five of them are in a box in her spare room. She has never told me why. She is not going to tell me a gift missed, and she never has.

Five failures. One she actually wears. Here is what was different about it.

The sixth pair was the [vrsn] Pain Relief Sneaker. Seven things about it turned out to matter.

Five pairs, about $535, all of it in one box in her spare room.

1She put them on and left them on

My mother gives a new pair one morning. If they pinch, they go in the box and I never hear about it. That is the whole test.

No break-in on these. Soft from the first step. She wore them into the kitchen and did not take them off.

See the pair she kept on →

2They do not look like old-lady shoes

The orthopedic pair was wide and molded. She thanked me in the voice that means the gift is already filed away.

Knit upper. Normal laces. Four colors. She wore them to lunch and nobody asked her about her shoes, which is the entire point.

3Her orthotics went straight in

She was fitted for orthotics years ago and she uses them. Every pair I bought asked her to give that up. Every pair got a polite no.

The insole in these lifts out. Hers drops in. A four-year argument, over in a second.

See how the insole comes out →

4They did not go flat

Everything soft I bought her packed down inside a month. Quietly, so nobody notices. She just goes back to holding the counter and blames her age.

Two layers in this sole. A soft one she feels, a firm one she does not. Month three still feels like the first morning.

5She stopped kicking them off

Every time she sat down. Shoes off, before she had finished sitting. I read it as a habit for years.

It was not a habit. It was relief. The front is cut wide, so her toes lie flat instead of stacking on each other. They stay on now until bed.

6She can put them in the wash

She gardens and will not admit to kneeling in mud. Every pale pair I ever bought her was ruined by April and quietly retired.

These go in the machine. Gentle, cold, air dry. They come out looking new, so there is one less reason to save them for good.

See the four colors →

7She asked me to order a second pair

For years she asked where we were going to park before agreeing to anything. She was calculating the walk, every single time. She stopped asking about a month in.

Then in the spring she asked me to order the beige ones as well.

My mother never asks me for anything. She asked for a second pair, and she tells her friends where they came from.

If you are not sure it is the shoes

Six things she does instead of telling you

Older adults often do not mention foot pain. They assume it is normal, or they are embarrassed, or they never see the bottom of their own feet. What families notice instead is a handful of small habits, and almost nobody connects them to footwear. If three of these sound like her, look in her closet before you look at her age.

She holds the furniture crossing a room
She has started avoiding the stairs
Her walk got slower, and shorter
She takes a moment before she stands up
She stopped coming to things she used to come to
Her shoes come off the moment she is home
